lesson.title: Plotting the Curve: Graphing Exponential Functions
lesson.summary: Graphing an exponential function y equals a times b raised to the x uses the same table-and-plot process as any other function, producing a curve that rises or falls smoothly and gets closer and closer to, but never touches, the x-axis.
lesson.body:
Graphing an exponential function uses the same basic process you already know from plotting points: choose several x-values, compute the matching y-value for each one, plot each resulting ordered pair on the coordinate plane, and connect them with a smooth curve. The one thing that changes is how the y-values are generated. In a linear function they come from repeated addition, so the points climb or fall in even steps. In an exponential function they come from repeated multiplication, so the points are not evenly spaced vertically, and the result is a curve rather than a straight line.

Worked example, growth: graph y equals 2 raised to the x. Build a table of values. At x equals negative 2, y equals 2 raised to the negative 2, which is 1 divided by 2 squared, which equals 0.25. At x equals negative 1, y equals 0.5. At x equals 0, y equals 1. At x equals 1, y equals 2. At x equals 2, y equals 4. At x equals 3, y equals 8. Plotting these points shows the curve hugging very close to the x-axis on the left side, since the y-values shrink toward zero as x decreases, without ever actually reaching zero, then crossing the y-axis at the point (0, 1), which confirms an initial value of 1, and then climbing increasingly steeply as x increases to the right.

Worked example, decay: graph y equals 3 times 0.5 raised to the x. At x equals 0, y equals 3 times 1, which is 3. At x equals 1, y equals 3 times 0.5, which is 1.5. At x equals 2, y equals 3 times 0.25, which is 0.75. At x equals 3, y equals 3 times 0.125, which is 0.375. Plotting these points shows a curve that starts at the y-intercept 3, the initial value, falls quickly at first, and then flattens out, getting closer and closer to the x-axis as x grows without ever crossing it.

A few features are worth checking on any exponential graph. The y-intercept, where the curve crosses the vertical axis at x equals 0, is always the initial value a. The horizontal line y equals 0 is a horizontal asymptote for these basic forms: the curve gets closer and closer to it forever but never touches or crosses it, since a positive number times any power of a positive base can never equal exactly zero. And the direction of the curve tells you the type of factor at a glance: rising left to right means a growth factor greater than 1, while falling left to right means a decay factor between 0 and 1. This smooth, ever-bending shape is the clearest visual way to see the difference between exponential functions and the straight lines of linear functions from the comparison in the previous chapter.
